status2026.detail: The APS Beamline Directory entry for 19-ID-E, fetched 2026-10-09, lists ISN as 'Operational/Accepting General Users' with access via on-site beamline staff (r6). The path there: technical commissioning of the endstation and KB optics in summer 2025 (r9). Stage 4, technical commissioning, on the 24 Nov 2025 APS progress graphic (r39). Stage 5, scientific commissioning and early experiments, on the 26 Jan 2026 graphic (r20). The Aug 2025 APS-U update had forecast first experiments 'either late this year or early next year' and general users 'either late in the first run of 2026 or sometime in the second run' (r19). A 31 Jul 2026 Argonne job posting still describes duties as 'commissioning and operation of the ISN' (r35). So 2026 is best read as early user operations with some commissioning still going on. The design target is a 20 nm spot at 25 keV. Abstracts from late 2025 and 2026 quote ~25-30 nm (r16, r17). For context, the APS Upgrade project as a whole was formally completed in early 2026 (r34), and Argonne's Sept 2026 nanoscience feature presents ISN as a powerful new in situ tool (r33).

tagline: A 220-meter X-ray microscope built to focus to about 20 nanometers while leaving room to heat, cool or charge the sample.
plainSummary: The In Situ Nanoprobe (ISN) is an X-ray microscope built to watch materials while they are working: a battery charging, a catalyst breathing hot gas, a solar cell forming in a furnace. It squeezes X-rays from the upgraded APS into a spot designed to be about 20 nanometers wide, roughly 4,500 times thinner than a human hair (early reports from commissioning quote 25-30 nm). Then it scans the sample through that spot. At each point it records which chemical elements glow back (X-ray fluorescence) and how the atoms are arranged (diffraction). It also records how the beam is scattered, which a computer turns into images designed to be sharper than 10 nm (ptychography), plus any electric current or visible light the X-rays trigger. The trick is distance. To get a tiny spot and still leave about 5-6 centimeters of free space for heaters, gas cells and liquid cells, the focusing mirrors have to be long. They also have to be lit by very orderly ('coherent') X-rays. So the beamline runs about 220 meters, out of the main ring building to a vibration-isolated concrete room in the new Long Beamline Building. There the air is held within ±0.05 °C over an hour and the instrument surfaces within ±0.01 °C.
expertSummary: ISN (19-ID-E) is a KB-mirror hard X-ray nanoprobe for 4.8-30 keV, built around a spatial filter. Source: two in-line revolver undulators (U21/U25, 112/94 periods each) and a windowless HHL front end with a 2x2 mm^2 exit mask at 25.4 m. In 19-ID-A, a flat water-cooled M1 (28 m) and a bendable M2 (29 m), both 2.5 mrad with Si/Cr/Pt stripes, focus vertically onto BDA-V at 55 m. An LN2-cooled horizontal Si(111) DCM (31.7 m) is paired with a designed Mo/B4C DMM (32.7 m, ~1% BW). M3 (35 m, Pt, inboard) focuses horizontally onto BDA-H at 64 m. The BDAs (down to ~3.5-4 µm) form an adjustable secondary source that filters upstream wavefront errors and optic motion. After ~147 m of 4-inch transport, a JTEC KB pair in UHV focuses the beam: KBV 404 mm (q = 396 mm), KBH 129 mm (q = 125.5 mm), θ = 2.5 mrad, NA ~1.7 mrad. Design result: a ~20 nm diffraction-limited focus at 25 keV with 61 mm optical working distance and >3x10^11 ph/s focused flux (design/abstract values; 2025-26 conference abstracts report ~25-30 nm at 25 keV, and no measured focused flux has been published). Stability requirements are 5/16 nrad (KBV/KBH) and 4 nm rms spot-sample motion. They are addressed with a 1 m isolated VC-G slab, ±0.01 °C surface control, flexure stages and 15-channel interferometry; preliminary KBV pitch noise is 0.4 nrad rms (measured in air with vacuum pumps off). Modalities: fly-scanned XRF and nano-XANES, ptychography, nano-XRD, XBIC/XBIV and XEOL, with in situ cells from 40 K to ~1000 °C, gas and liquid flow, and bias.

whatAPSUEnables.plain: A nanoprobe can only use the orderly, 'coherent' part of an X-ray beam to make its smallest spot. Everything else gets thrown away at a pair of tiny slits. The old APS electron beam was about 275 micrometers wide, so very little of its light was coherent. The upgraded ring squeezes it to about 15 micrometers. That leaves far more usable photons. ISN can make a 20 nm spot and still have enough X-rays to scan big samples quickly. It can also do this at high energies that pass through cell windows, water and gas while the sample is changing.
whatAPSUEnables.expert: Diffraction-limited KB focusing accepts only about one transverse coherent mode in each plane. The BDAs are closed to roughly the coherence-matched size, Δ ≈ 0.44 λ z / A, where A is the KB acceptance. So the focused flux scales with the source's coherent flux, not its total flux. The MBA lattice brings the horizontal emittance down to ~30-40 pm·rad, and <30 pm·rad has been measured (r29). That is within a factor of ~4-10 of the photon diffraction limit λ/4π (3.9 pm at 25 keV, 9.9 pm at 10 keV; my calculation). Before the upgrade the emittance was ~70x larger (r14). The upgrade is what makes the ISN layout possible. A 220 m geometry and long KB mirrors (~1.0 mm vertical acceptance) give a 61 mm working distance. Upstream optics sit entirely before the BDAs, so their wavefront errors and nanoradian motions are filtered out. There is also high coherent flux at 20-30 keV for penetrating in situ cells. Two revolver undulators make the U21 structure available to boost brilliance at the high-energy end (r3).
quantitative: Electron beam size shrinks from ~275 µm (H) x 10 µm (V) before the upgrade to ~15 µm x 4 µm in brightness mode; brightness up to 500x (r30)
Horizontal source size reduced ~20x (r1, sec. 4-7.1); measured horizontal emittance <30 pm·rad by grating interferometry at 3-ID-B (r29); pre-upgrade to APS-U emittance reduction ~70-fold (r14)
Coherent flux after the BDAs: 7.2x10^12 ph/s at 10 keV (coherent fraction 5.58%) and 4.7x10^11 ph/s at 25 keV (0.94%) (r1, Table 4.51)
Design focused flux at 25 keV: 3.4x10^11 ph/s coherent into 16x16 nm^2 FWHM, or 3.1x10^12 ph/s into 24x30 nm^2 with the BDAs open (r1, Table 4.52)
Design focused flux at 10 keV: 3.5x10^12 ph/s coherent into 39x39 nm^2, or 8.9x10^12 ph/s into 43x52 nm^2 (r1, Table 4.52)
JACoW abstract of the MEDSI'25 paper: focused flux >3x10^11 ph/s at 25 keV (r9). This restates the design capability (cf. FDR 3.4x10^11 ph/s coherent); the paper itself reports no measured flux
2017 design estimate: focused-flux gain of 10^3-10^4 over pre-upgrade nanoprobes for spectroscopy (0.01% BW), and 10^4-10^5 for elemental mapping and ptychography (1% BW) (r3)

KB mirrors vs diffractive optics: ~10x higher focusing efficiency at 10 keV and ~100x at 30 keV; DMM plus non-chromatic KB gives ~25x more flux than the DCM where chemical-state contrast is not needed (r3)
Expected reduction in acquisition time: a factor of 100 or more (r16)

techniques.name: Scanning X-ray fluorescence microscopy and fluorescence tomography
techniques.plain: When the X-ray spot hits an atom, the atom gives off its own X-ray 'color'. Each element has its own fingerprint color. Scanning the spot across the sample builds a map of where every element sits, down to trace amounts. Rotating the sample turns these maps into 3D.
techniques.expert: Energy-dispersive detection uses a Hitachi 7-element SDD or a RaySpec 12-element backscatter SDD with Xspress3 Mk2 readout (r9). The 2017 design called for ~125 eV resolution at Mn Kα and up to 10^8 counts/s (r3). Scans are fly scans: up to 1 mm/s for horizontal lines (and vertical lines when the ROI is <90 µm), 0.1 mm/s for vertical scans over ROIs up to 10 mm, with a 2 kg payload over 10x10 mm (r9). A Micronix PR-160 rotation stage provides 3D. Capacitive sensors on a diamond-turned reference ring correct runout and wobble at ~20 nm (r9). Because mirrors are non-chromatic, 1% bandwidth from the DMM can be used for mapping (r3). Ptychographic recovery of the probe allows XRF maps to be deconvolved to ~10 nm (r3).

techniques.name: XRF nanospectroscopy (nano-XANES spectromicroscopy)
techniques.plain: Tuning the X-ray energy step by step across an element's absorption edge shows its chemical state, for example rusted versus metallic iron. ISN can do this in a 20 nm spot, so it can tell the chemistry of one tiny particle from its neighbor.
techniques.expert: The LN2-cooled Si(111) H-DCM (ΔE/E ≈ 1.4x10^-4) scans energy (r6). The KB focus is achromatic, so the spot and the sample position do not move during an energy scan and no focusing optic needs re-tuning (r3); the undulator gap and the DCM angle still track the energy. M1 has a side notch with cooling above it to suppress thermal deformation. The design shows <2% flux change in a 10 µm BDA-V when the undulator is scanned from 5.0 to 5.1 keV (r1). The energy range covers K edges from Ti (4.97 keV) through the 3d and 4d transition metals up to Sn (29.20 keV; Sb at 30.49 keV is just out of range), plus L3 edges of the rare earths (5.48 keV for La to 9.24 keV for Lu) and of heavy elements such as Pb and Bi (r1, r3; edge energies are standard tabulated values).

techniques.name: Ptychography (2D and 3D coherent diffractive imaging)
techniques.plain: Instead of only counting X-rays, a camera far behind the sample records the speckle pattern each overlapping spot makes. A computer works backward from thousands of these patterns to an image sharper than the spot itself. The design goal is below 10 nanometers for thin, see-through samples.
techniques.expert: The diffraction-limited focus is intrinsically coherent, so ptychography can run alongside XRF on every transparent sample (r3). The design goal was sub-10 nm resolution (r1, r13). An Eiger2 X 1M sits on a downstream XYZ table with 6 m of travel along the beam. The same detector serves ptychography, SAXS and absorption measurements (r9). Planned data rates are ~5 GB/s at ~3 kHz average frame rate, about 10 PB of raw data per year across ISN (r25). Data stream to ALCF's Aurora for processing (r9). Ptychography also returns the complex KB probe, which is useful for diagnosing optics.

techniques.name: Nano-diffraction / X-ray diffraction microscopy
techniques.plain: Crystals scatter (diffract) X-rays into bright spots at specific angles. A robot arm swings a camera around the sample to catch them, revealing which crystal phase is present at each point and how it changes as the sample is heated or charged.
techniques.expert: An Eiger2 X 1M is carried by a Stäubli TX2-160L robot so it can be positioned in spherical coordinates (r9). Diffracted beams leave the sample chamber through a 0.5 mm Materion Be dome window. The window is tipped 10° above the beam plane and 25° outboard, has a 152 mm clear aperture and passes ~0.25 sr (r9). The PDR set out to cover a few degrees to ~80° horizontally and 45-60° vertically (r3). Diffraction is described as an auxiliary contrast for tracking phase changes during in situ work (r13; FDR 4-7.7.4 lists 'structural imaging' as auxiliary, r1). The 2020 design Be window gave a 7-60° vertical and -5 to 60° horizontal diffraction cone (r10).

techniques.name: X-ray beam induced current / voltage
techniques.plain: In a solar cell or LED, the X-ray spot frees electrons like a tiny flashlight. Measuring the current or voltage at each spot shows which nanoscale regions work well and which defects kill performance.
techniques.expert: Current and voltage are read by a CAEN ELS TetrAMM electrometer (r9; how it is triggered during fly scans is not described publicly). XBIC/XBIV is collected pixel by pixel together with XRF, which correlates composition and defects with local charge collection (r3, r4).

techniques.name: X-ray excited optical luminescence microscopy
techniques.plain: Some materials glow with visible or infrared light when X-rays hit them. ISN has a built-in optical microscope that collects this glow, so scientists can link light emission (for example, from a perovskite or LED material) to the chemistry at the same spot.
techniques.expert: A custom in-line vacuum microscope sits just upstream of the sample. It uses a NIR 10X/0.26 NA objective and a fold mirror with a hole that lets the X-rays pass. Field of view is 600 µm with 1 µm resolution (r9). A motorized path selector collects 430-1800 nm emission into a fiber-coupled spectrometer. An external light module (Optique Peter) can inject excitation or bias light (r9).

scienceCases.title: Watching a solar-cell absorber form
scienceCases.plain: Thin-film solar cells such as CIGS are 'cooked' at about 600 °C in selenium vapor. Tiny defects that form along the way can ruin efficiency. ISN can follow where copper, indium, gallium and selenium move while the film is being made, nanometer by nanometer.
scienceCases.expert: The design case is in situ selenization or sulfurization of Cu(In,Ga) precursors under H2Se, or H2S over Se-capped films, while temperature changes. XRF, XBIC and XEOL are correlated pixel by pixel to follow defect formation (r3, r4). A pre-upgrade demonstration at 600 °C took ~7 min per 10x10 µm map (r3). ISN aims to cut map times by more than 100x, with doses low enough for beam-sensitive halide perovskites (r4, r16).

scienceCases.title: Battery particles, one crystallite at a time
scienceCases.plain: Battery electrodes are powders of tiny crystals. Some take up lithium faster than others, and some crack or degrade. ISN can map the chemistry of individual particles while the battery charges and discharges, to find the first ones that fail.
scienceCases.expert: Example: LMFP olivine cathodes, where primary crystallites are 25-200 nm. Fast nano-XANES with a 20 nm beam, plus auxiliary XRD, can resolve mixed phases within a crystallite during cycling (r4). An as-built Hummingbird electrochemical holder has two fluid inlets, heating above 100 °C, bulk electrodes and a flow cell thicker than 200 µm. It rotates for tomography (r9). The APS feature page uses battery defects as its illustrative example (r5).

scienceCases.title: Catalysts caught in the act
scienceCases.plain: Most fuels and chemicals are made with catalysts, and catalysts change shape and chemistry once they are taken out of the reactor. ISN's gas cell heats samples to about 1000 °C in flowing gas, so scientists can see the active metals as they really are while they work.
scienceCases.expert: Targets in the design studies (r4): metal poisoning (Fe, Ni) in fluid-catalytic-cracking particles; the chemical state near grain boundaries of Cu CO2-reduction electrocatalysts under bias; buried interfaces in photo-electrochemical devices. The as-built Hummingbird catalysis and synthesis holder has two pressure-controlled gas inlets, four bias channels and heating to 1000 °C with low drift (r9).

scienceCases.title: Finding stray atoms in next-generation chips
scienceCases.plain: Modern transistors are only a few nanometers wide. A few misplaced metal atoms can make the insulation between them fail. ISN's hard X-rays see through a whole intact chip and can spot traces of metal at the 0.1% level in tiny regions.
scienceCases.expert: The 2017 science case targets dopants, impurities and defects in intact 3D device stacks. Examples are high-k dielectrics and Cu/Co back-end-of-line interconnects at the 7 nm node and beyond. ISN is described as the only non-destructive tool sensitive to impurities at ≤0.1% in small regions of an intact system (r4).

scienceCases.title: Electrochemical interfaces for fuel cells and electrolyzers
scienceCases.plain: Fuel cells and water electrolyzers rely on thin layers of precious metals whose structure shifts as they run. ISN can watch these layers in liquid, under voltage, at the 10-100 nanometer scale where the changes start.
scienceCases.expert: Proposals from the 2023 ISN/PtychoProbe first-experiments workshop (r18) include: (1) imaging the distribution of functional phases in PEM fuel-cell and electrolyzer electrodes during fabrication and operation; (2) resolving composition dynamics of partial Au and Pt films on Ir(hkl) over 10-100 nm, where surface diffusion is faster in electrolyte than in gas; (3) vacancy formation in 2D TMD H2-evolution catalysts. The proposals were made for both ISN and PtychoProbe; the Au/Pt-on-Ir abstract names a purpose-built in situ electrochemical cell as the key enabler, which is where ISN's long working distance matters.

scienceCases.title: Environmental and quantum materials
scienceCases.plain: The same tool can look for valuable metals and toxic elements in coal ash, follow microbes interacting with minerals, or cool quantum materials to minus 233 °C (40 K) to see how tiny regions behave.
scienceCases.expert: Workshop topics (r18) include nanoscale characterization of coal-ash resource potential and environmental risk, in situ crystallization of epitaxial complex oxides, and driven dynamics in quantum materials. The PDR also points to the earth and environmental community: microbes at soil and gas interfaces, and subsurface carbon sequestration (r3). An APS-built closed-cycle He (ARS) cryostat holder covers 40-355 K with feedback control and is designed for ultralow vibration (r9, still in development at publication).

insertionDevices.name: APS21R25#1 (upstream revolver undulator)
insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid permanent-magnet revolver undulator (two magnet structures on a rotating strongback)
insertionDevices.notes: Selectable structures: APS21#6, 2.1 cm x 112 periods (Keff 1.38, E1 8.35 keV at 8.5 mm), or APS25#5, 2.5 cm x 94 periods (Keff 2.00, E1 4.56 keV). Length is my estimate from N x period (2.35 m), consistent with the nominal 2.4 m inline devices (r2). Gap specs: 8.5 mm minimum gap, 5 mm maximum taper, revolve only with the gap open (r2). U25 covers the 4.8 keV low end continuously. U21 boosts brilliance at high energy (r3).

insertionDevices.name: APS21R25#2 (downstream revolver undulator)
insertionDevices.notes: Selectable structures: APS21#7, 2.1 cm x 112 periods, or APS25#2, 2.5 cm x 94 periods. periodMm here is illustrative: either structure can be active. FDR Table 3.13 lists a phase shifter/corrector between the two in-line devices to keep them in phase (r2).

source.canting: none (dual in-line, not canted; phase shifter/corrector between devices per FDR Table 3.13)
source.frontEnd: Standard APS-U high-heat-load front end (HHLFE), based on the 28-ID design (r2). Rated 21 kW total and 590 kW/mrad^2 peak. Windowless exit via a differential pumping section (r2, r3). Components: clearing magnet, burn-through fixed mask, fixed masks, photon shutter with intensity monitor IM1, GRID XBPM1, safety shutters, and an exit mask with XBPM2 (r2). ISN exit mask: 2x2 mm^2 at 25.4 m, then a 5x5 mm^2 exit collimator at 26.1 m (r1). Up to 2.28 kW passes the mask (r1).
source.sourceSizeAndDivergence: Nominal APS-U ID electron-beam source at zero current (r8). Flat-beam mode (κ=0.1): σx = 14.5 µm, σx' = 2.75 µrad, σy = 3.1 µm, σy' = 1.29 µrad. Round-beam mode: σx = 12.3 µm, σx' = 2.34 µrad, σy = 8.3 µm, σy' = 3.47 µrad. Single-electron photon contribution at 25 keV for L ≈ 4.7 m (my calculation, σr = √(2λL)/4π, σr' = √(λ/2L)): ≈1.7 µm and ≈2.3 µrad. Which mode a given run uses changes the vertical source size and therefore the BDA-V settings.

branches.name: ISN nanoprobe line (single branch)
branches.description: One monochromatic branch: two revolver undulators → windowless HHL front end → 19-ID-A (M1, M2, DCM/DMM, M3) → 19-ID-C (BDA-V at 55 m) → 19-ID-D (BDA-H at 64 m, shutter) → ~147 m transport → 19-ID-E in the Long Beamline Building (KB nanofocus at 220 m, beamstop at 227 m). The instrument is fixed in location and runs only in fixed-exit, KB-focused monochromatic mode (FDR 4-7.7.4).

components.name: Upstream revolver undulator (APS21R25#1)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: two ~2.35 m devices with a phase shifter between them share the ~4.8 m straight. Center placed ~1.2 m upstream of the straight-section center (source point = 0).
components.plain: A row of strong magnets that wiggles the electrons to make an intense X-ray beam. It has two magnet sets on a rotating holder, so operators can swap 'gears' for low or high X-ray energy.
components.expert: Hybrid PM revolver with 2.1 cm/112-period and 2.5 cm/94-period structures (Keff 1.38/2.00 at 8.5 mm). Gap minimum 8.5 mm (user minimum 8.7 mm). Per device at min gap and 200 mA: 5.4 kW (U21) or 8.1 kW (U25).

components.name: Phase shifter / corrector
components.distanceNote: Approximate: between the two in-line undulators near the straight-section center (inferred from FDR Table 3.13).
components.plain: A small magnet section between the two undulators that delays the electrons slightly, so the light from both adds up in step.
components.expert: FDR Table 3.13 lists a 'phase shifter/corrector' for 19-ID dual in-line revolvers. Required because the optimal phasing varies with gap (FDR 3-3.3.6). As-built implementation not confirmed in public sources.

components.name: Downstream revolver undulator (APS21R25#2)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (see upstream device).
components.plain: The second undulator, identical to the first. Two in a row roughly double the brightness.
components.expert: Structures APS21#7 (2.1 cm) and APS25#2 (2.5 cm). Total magnetic length of the pair ≈ 4.7 m (FDR: 'revolver undulator of 4.6 m length').

components.name: High-heat-load front end (HHLFE)
components.distanceNote: Schematic placeholder: the front end runs inside the storage-ring tunnel from roughly 14 m to the FOE at ~24-26 m. No 19-ID-specific positions are published apart from the exit mask and collimator. The windowless exit uses a differential pumping section, placed at ~25.5 m in the 2017 PDR layout (r3).
components.plain: The 'airlock and safety gate' between the accelerator and the beamline. It soaks up excess heat, can block the beam, and measures where the beam points.
components.expert: APS-U HHLFE based on the 28-ID design: 21 kW / 590 kW/mrad^2 limits. Includes a clearing magnet, burn-through fixed mask (BTFM1), photon shutter with IM1, GRID XBPM1 (required AC 0.01-1000 Hz resolution 3.7 µm H / 2.4 µm V, FDR Table 3.4), and safety shutters. ISN uses a windowless differential-pumping exit to preserve wavefront quality.

components.name: Front-end exit mask (with XBPM2)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.plain: A thick metal block with a 2 mm square hole. Only the bright central core of the X-ray fan gets through.
components.expert: Standard HHL exit mask, 2x2 mm^2 (H x V) aperture. Transmits up to 2.28 kW at Ky = 1.939 (FDR Table 4.48). XBPM2 is integrated into the exit mask (FDR ch. 3). The 2020 shielding study used a 2 (H) x 1 (V) mm aperture.

components.name: Front-end exit collimator
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.plain: A heavy-metal block that stops stray high-energy radiation from the accelerator while letting the X-ray beam through.
components.expert: Standard HHL front-end exit (bremsstrahlung) collimator. Aperture narrowed to 5x5 mm^2 for APS-U small-offset monochromators.

components.name: White-beam slits (19ID-SL-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49. A small pump stand (RGA, gauges) sits at 27.3 m.
components.plain: Adjustable jaws that trim the raw 'white' X-ray beam before it hits the first mirror.
components.expert: HHL tilting-type white-beam slits. They set the illuminated length and total power on M1. Per the PDR, the WBS defines beam size and power for the mirror system.

components.name: M1 flat high-heat-load mirror (19ID-MR-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49 (Knopp 2018 also gives 28 m). M1 and M2 share one vacuum vessel in the FOE drawing (NIMA 2020 Fig. 3a).
components.plain: The first mirror skims the beam at a tiny angle. It removes unwanted high-energy X-rays and absorbs most of the heat, up to about 450 watts.
components.expert: Flat Si mirror, 400x50x50 mm (r12), water-cooled, downward reflecting at 2.5 mrad (5 mrad deflection). Bare Si, Cr and Pt stripes, selected by horizontal translation, for harmonic rejection across 4.8-30 keV. Absorbs up to 455 W, peak 1.16 W/mm^2. Thermal slope error <0.05 µrad after correction. Side-notch cooling cuts thermal deformation ~10x.

components.name: M2 bendable vertical focusing mirror (19ID-MR-2)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.plain: A second mirror that bends the beam back level and gently focuses it down onto a tiny slit 26 meters away.
components.expert: Upward-reflecting, water-cooled, mechanically bent pink-beam mirror at 2.5 mrad, same three stripes as M1. Focuses vertically, near 1:1, onto BDA-V at 55 m. FDR: bending radius as small as ~10 km, which matches pure 29 m to 55 m focusing (R = 2pq/((p+q)θ) ≈ 11 km, my calculation). The bend also corrects the thermal bumps of M1 and M2; MEDSI'18 FEA needed a 4.38 km radius at 5 keV, the worst heat-load case (r12). The two sources disagree on the minimum radius. Absorbs ~13 W.

components.name: Secondary bremsstrahlung collimator (19ID-SC-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49 (listed at 29.7 m together with PM-1).
components.plain: Shielding that stops stray radiation that follows the old straight-through path.
components.expert: Secondary bremsstrahlung collimator downstream of the mirror pair.

components.name: Photon mask / white-beam stop (19ID-PM-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.plain: Catches the part of the beam that did not bounce off the mirrors. Only the mirror-reflected 'pink' beam continues, about 5 mm lower.
components.expert: Pink-beam aperture and white-beam stop. Accommodates the vertical offset after M1/M2: about 5 mm downward from 5 mrad x 1.0 m, my geometric estimate.

components.name: Diagnostic flag (19ID-BD-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.plain: A pop-in screen that glows where the beam hits, so staff can see and align it.
components.expert: Diagnostic flag assembly downstream of the mirror pair.

components.name: Pink-beam slits (19ID-SL-2)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.plain: Jaws that limit the size and heat of the beam reaching the monochromators.
components.expert: Pink slits, CUFE tilting type.

components.name: Double-crystal monochromator, LN2-cooled H-DCM (19ID-MN-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49 (FOE drawing places it at ~31.4 m).
components.plain: Two perfect silicon crystals pick out one X-ray color (energy) at a time. Tilting them tunes the energy for chemical-state scans.
components.expert: Small-offset Si(111) DCM, LN2-cooled, fixed exit, horizontally deflecting (inboard). Crystal motions are minimized for inter-crystal angular stability (~0.1 µrad target per PDR Table 6.25, r3). Horizontal geometry protects the vertical wavefront but costs some π-polarization reflectivity (83% at 5 keV per the PDR, r3). ΔE/E ≈ 1.4x10^-4. Incident pink-beam power after M1/M2 is ~80 W (5 keV case).

components.name: Double-multilayer monochromator (19ID-MN-2)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49 (FOE drawing places it at ~32.5 m). As-built status unconfirmed: the beamline directory lists only the H-DCM.
components.plain: A 'wide-band' alternative to the crystals. It lets about 1% of colors through, giving about 25 times more X-rays for fast element maps where chemistry is not needed.
components.expert: Design: Mo/B4C, d = 25 Å (9/16 Å), 300 bilayers. Conservative alternative: d = 20 Å, 600 bilayers (40% narrower BW, -15% reflectance). LN2-cooled, fixed exit, flexure-guided, horizontally deflecting inboard. Delivers ~11.6 W to each BDA in the worst case.

components.name: Pink-beam missteering mask (19ID-PM-2)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.plain: A safety mask that catches the beam if it is ever steered the wrong way.
components.expert: Photon mask against pink-beam missteering.

components.name: Primary bremsstrahlung collimator (19ID-BC-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.plain: Lead shielding that keeps the most energetic stray radiation inside the first hutch.
components.expert: Lead primary bremsstrahlung collimator.

components.name: Pink-beam slits (19ID-SL-3)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.plain: Jaws that set the beam footprint on the horizontal mirror.
components.expert: Pink slits, tilting type, upstream of M3.

components.name: M3 horizontal focusing mirror (19ID-MR-3)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49; the NIMA 2020 FOE drawing shows M3 at the downstream end of 19-ID-A. NOTE: FDR Fig. 4.40 (and the 2017 PDR) label this mirror at 43 m, which is superseded.
components.plain: A mirror that steers the beam slightly sideways and focuses it onto the second tiny slit 29 meters downstream.
components.expert: Inboard-deflecting, bendable, Pt-coated mirror at 2.5 mrad (5 mrad deflection). Focuses horizontally onto BDA-H at 64 m and accepts beam from either the DCM or the DMM. Slope error <0.1 µrad; radius as small as ~11 km. Vertical translation selects the stripe. Consistency check (my calculation): focusing onto 64 m needs R = 2pq/((p+q)θ) ≈ 12.7 km from 35 m but ≈ 11.3 km from 43 m, so the FDR's '~11 km' matches the older 43 m layout. With M3 at 35 m the horizontal source is imaged nearly 1:1 (0.83x) rather than demagnified 2x as in the PDR.

components.name: Shielded transport 19-ID-A to 19-ID-C (19ID-ST-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact span 35.8-48.2 m (FDR Table 4.49); midpoint given. The FDR table says 'to 19-ID-B', but the FDR's own optics text places BDA-V 'in enclosure C' and the NIMA 2020 plan labels the hutch 19-ID-C, so 'B' looks like a table error.
components.plain: A lead-shielded pipe that carries the beam safely across the experiment floor between hutches.
components.expert: Lead-shielded vacuum transport, 12.4 m long.

components.name: Missteering mask and bremsstrahlung collimator/stop (19ID-PM-3, 19ID-BC-2)
components.distanceNote: Exact: PM-3 at 49.1 m, BC-2 at 49.5 m (FDR Table 4.49); one hotspot at 49.3 m.
components.plain: Safety blocks at the entrance of the aperture hutch.
components.expert: Pink-beam missteering mask plus lead primary bremsstrahlung collimator/stop.

components.name: Vertical beam-defining aperture, BDA-V (19ID-SL-4)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49; consistent with the NIMA 2020 plan (scaled).
components.plain: A slit only a few micrometers tall, narrower than a red blood cell. The focused beam passes through it and it becomes a new, perfectly clean 'mini source' for the microscope. Closing it gives sharper focus but fewer X-rays.
components.expert: Water-cooled vertical aperture at the M2 focus (2017 PDR: vertical secondary-source size ~4.4-6.6 µm). Must reach ~3.5-4 µm with resolution, accuracy and stability to match. It must block 30 keV photons outside the opening (the FDR literally says 'less than 99% ... blocked', apparently meaning <1% transmitted). Gets ~0.2 W with the DCM and up to ~11.6 W with the DMM; at normal incidence the slit would exceed 850 K, so jaws need a grazing-incidence surface. Filters upstream vibration and wavefront errors.

components.name: Horizontal beam-defining aperture, BDA-H (19ID-SL-5)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49; consistent with the NIMA 2020 plan (scaled).
components.plain: The matching side-to-side slit. Together the two slits act as a 'pinhole' that turns the big source into a tiny, steady one.
components.expert: Water-cooled horizontal aperture at the M3 focus (2017 PDR: horizontal secondary-source size ~16-18 µm). Minimum aperture ~4 µm. Example settings: 13.0 x 4.1 µm^2 (H x V) for fully coherent 16x16 nm focus at 25 keV (FDR Fig. 4.41). The PDR used 19 x 6 µm for a 19.6 x 19.8 nm spot. The PDR also required a removable beam flag downstream of the last BDA and beam position monitors after each BDA (r3); their as-built form is not published.

components.name: Photon shutter (19ID-SH-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.plain: A heavy safety door for X-rays. It closes so people can enter the endstation while the rest of the beamline stays on.
components.expert: P9-50 water-cooled pink-beam shutter. Rated for pink beam because a monochromator-retracted beam (one or three mirror reflections) could reach the long transport (cf. NIMA 2020 scenarios).

components.name: Long shielded mono-beam transport (19ID-ST-2)
components.distanceNote: Exact span 65.5-213.0 m (FDR Table 4.49); midpoint given. Shielded ion-pump stations at 95, 124, 153 and 183 m.
components.enclosure: Experiment hall, LOM area and enclosed corridor to the Long Beamline Building
components.plain: About 147 meters of steel pipe, as long as one and a half football fields. It carries the beam in vacuum out of the ring building to the separate microscope building.
components.expert: ~146 m of shielded transport, 4-inch inner diameter. Four 200 L/s ion pumps are spaced along it with 100 L/s pumps at the ends; the MolFlow model (outgassing 3x10^-10 mbar·L/s/cm²) predicted ~2x10^-7 mbar at the pumps rising to ~1x10^-6 mbar midway between them, and up to ~8x10^-6 mbar with two pumps failed (MEDSI 2018 talk, r26, slide 10). Pump stations sit in shielded mini-enclosures. The pipe is wide enough that a mirror-only (pink) beam could reach hutch E, so E is shielded for that case (r14).

components.name: Double Si3N4 exit window (19ID-WN-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.plain: Two ultra-thin ceramic windows that separate the beamline vacuum from the endstation.
components.expert: Double Si3N4 window. Windows are kept to the endstation to preserve coherence; the front end is windowless.

components.name: Attenuator / filter box (19ID-FL-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.plain: Thin metal foils that can be slid into the beam to dim it for delicate samples.
components.expert: X-ray filters for attenuation, part of the endstation beam-conditioning section on granite blocks in low vacuum.

components.name: Beam-conditioning section: scintillator BPMs, clean-up slits, PIN diodes
components.distanceNote: Approximate: between the window (213.0 m) and the KB optics (~219.6 m), on granite blocks (MEDSI'25 Fig. 3). No individual positions published.
components.plain: Cameras and sensors that check the beam's position and brightness just before the microscope, plus slits that trim stray light.
components.expert: Two scintillator beam-position monitors, clean-up slits and two PIN diodes for flux. Mounted on large granite blocks for stability; mostly low vacuum.

components.name: Fast shutter (19ID-FS-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.plain: A quick-acting shutter that only lets X-rays hit the sample while data are being taken, to limit radiation damage.
components.expert: Fast shutter in the endstation beam-conditioning line.

components.name: Vertical nanofocusing KB mirror (KBV)
components.distanceNote: Derived: q_v = 396 mm upstream of the 220.0 m focus (MEDSI'25 Fig. 5a); p = 165.004 m from BDA-V at 55 m.
components.plain: A 40 cm mirror polished to within a few atoms of a perfect curve. It focuses the beam vertically to about 20 nm at a point 40 cm away.
components.expert: JTEC elliptical-cylinder mirror on Si(100): 404 mm long, θ = 2.5 mrad, p = 165.004 m, q = 396 mm. Accepts ~1.0 mm of beam; NA ≈ 1.67 mrad at 25 keV. Spec: figure error <2.0 nm (metric not stated), roughness <0.15 nm rms (FDR target: rms height error <0.38 nm). Pitch stability 5 nrad required, 0.4 nrad rms measured. Pitch is driven differentially by two APS weak-link vertical flexure stages (r10, r11; design aim 1 nm / 5 nrad) with laser-interferometer and capacitive sensors. MEDSI'25 Fig. 5b lists 0.6 nrad fine resolution over a 10 µrad fine range and ±3 mrad coarse range (r9). MEDSI'25 drawing shows it reflecting upward.

components.name: Horizontal nanofocusing KB mirror (KBH)
components.distanceNote: Derived: q_h = 125.5 mm upstream of the 220.0 m focus (MEDSI'25 Fig. 5a).
components.plain: A shorter mirror that focuses side to side. It stops 6 cm before the sample, leaving room for heaters and gas cells.
components.expert: JTEC mirror, 129 mm long, q = 125.5 mm, 4 mm gap after KBV. Working distance 61 mm from the mirror end to the focus. NA ≈ 1.74 mrad at 25 keV (FDR). Mounted on a gantry so the sample chamber fits underneath (MEDSI'20, r10). Stability 16 nrad required. FDR target rms height error <0.45 nm.

components.name: Square pinhole (scatter guard) after the KB mirrors
components.distanceNote: Approximate: 'a square pinhole after the KB mirrors' (MEDSI'25); exact position not published.
components.plain: A tiny square opening that blocks stray light reflected by the mirror edges, so only the focused beam reaches the sample.
components.expert: Cleans up unfocused and singly reflected beam components between the KB optics and the sample.

components.name: In-line vacuum optical microscope (XEOL / alignment)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: 'just upstream of the sample' (MEDSI'25).
components.plain: A built-in light microscope that looks along the X-ray beam through a mirror with a hole in it. Users can see the sample and catch any light it emits.
components.expert: NIR 10X/0.26 NA infinity-corrected objective on XYZ stages. Fold mirror with a hole for the X-rays; FOV 600 µm, 1 µm resolution. Motorized path selector sends 430-1800 nm emission to a fiber spectrometer, and an Optique Peter module injects light.

components.name: Sample scanning stack and metrology (ISN instrument 19ID-BI-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact nominal focus: FDR Table 4.49, MEDSI'25. Design geometry gives ~220.4 m.
components.plain: The sample rides on a stack of ultra-precise motors that sweep it through the beam at up to 1 mm per second. Laser rulers check every nanometer of motion.
components.expert: XYZ stack with 10 mm^3 travel: Aerotech PRO225SL (along beam), ANT130L (transverse), APS vertical flexure stage with stepper and piezo, plus a Micronix PR-160 rotation. Quasi-Maxwell kinematic holder mount 60 mm below the beam; max envelope 24 mm diameter cylinder; 2 kg payload. 15-channel interferometry to Invar/Zerodur frames; spot-sample stability 4 nm rms required. Chamber can run high vacuum, air or inert gas, with single-crystal diamond windows and a 2 mm He gap to the UHV optics chamber. A granite table with motorized air bearing handles coarse alignment.

components.name: In situ sample environments
components.distanceNote: At the sample position.
components.plain: Swap-in mini-labs: a liquid cell for batteries and electrochemistry, a hot gas cell up to 1000 °C for catalysts, and a cryostat down to 40 K.
components.expert: Three rotatable holders: (1) Hummingbird Scientific electrochemistry (two fluid inlets, >100 °C, bulk electrodes, >200 µm flow cell); (2) Hummingbird gas/heating (two pressure-controlled gas inlets, four bias channels, up to 1000 °C); (3) APS-built cryo holder, 40-355 K with a closed-cycle ARS He cryostat, in development. A gas-handling system for reactive gases was planned for the endstation (PDR). The 2017 PDR had planned cooling to 10 K; the as-built cryo holder starts at 40 K (r3, r9).

specs.media: vacuum, air, inert gas, flowing gas/liquid

components.name: Fluorescence detectors: 7-element SDD and 12-element backscatter SDD
components.distanceNote: At the sample (side/backscatter ports).
components.plain: Detectors that sort the X-rays given off by the sample by energy, revealing which elements are present at each point.
components.expert: Hitachi 7-element SDD or RaySpec 12-element backscatter SDD with Xspress3 Mk2. The 2020 design had two SDD ports 'oriented at 15° and 0° from X' (the instrument X axis, not the beam axis); the 0° port is for the backscatter detector and the 15° port was designed for a multi-element or larger confocal detector (r10).

components.name: XBIC/XBIV electrometer
components.distanceNote: At the sample (electrical feedthroughs).
components.plain: A very sensitive current meter wired to the sample to measure the electricity the X-rays create.
components.expert: CAEN ELS TetrAMM 4-channel picoammeter for beam-induced current and voltage maps.

components.name: Diffraction detector on robot arm (Eiger2 X 1M)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: robot-positioned around and above the sample (MEDSI'25 Fig. 3); variable.
components.plain: A camera on an industrial robot arm that swings around the sample to catch X-rays bounced off crystals.
components.expert: Dectris Eiger2 X 1M on a Stäubli TX2-160L in spherical coordinates. Views through a 0.5 mm Be dome window (Materion) tipped 10° up and 25° outboard: 152 mm clear aperture, ~0.25 sr.

components.name: Forward ptychography / SAXS detector on 6 m table (Eiger2 X 1M)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: on a downstream XYZ table with 6 m travel along the beam (≈220.5-226.5 m); midpoint shown.
components.plain: A camera straight downstream that records the speckle pattern of the beam. A computer turns it into images sharper than the X-ray spot.
components.expert: Dectris Eiger2 X 1M on an XYZ motion table with 6 m longitudinal travel, for forward-scattering ptychography, SAXS and absorption. The PDR asked for multi-kHz frame rates and >20-bit dynamic range. The 2024 APS computing plan assumed ~3 kHz average frame rate and ~5 GB/s for this detector (r25).

components.name: Mono beamstop (19ID-BS-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49; drawn on the downstream wall of the concrete hutch (NIMA 2020 Fig. 3b).
components.plain: The end of the line: a block that safely absorbs whatever is left of the beam.
components.expert: Monochromatic beamstop on the downstream wall of the 19-ID-E concrete enclosure.

enclosures.name: Storage-ring tunnel / front end
enclosures.role: accelerator tunnel housing the undulators (straight section) and HHL front end
enclosures.notes: Source point = center of the ID straight. The FOE upstream wall is ~24 m, scaled from the NIMA 2020 plan; the FE exit mask is at 25.4 m inside the FOE.

enclosures.name: 19-ID-A
enclosures.role: first optics enclosure (white/pink beam): M1+M2 tank, DCM, DMM, M3
enclosures.notes: Approx from NIMA 2020 Fig. 2 scaled to FDR distances (~64 px/m at 400 dpi). The end wall matches the 35.8 m start of transport ST-1. Trapezoidal footprint, roughly 1.9-2.4 m wide inside and wider downstream. The PDR planned to reuse the SBC-era 19-ID-A/B as the FOE.

enclosures.name: 19-ID-C
enclosures.role: aperture hutch 1 (monochromatic): PM-3, BC-2, vertical BDA at 55 m
enclosures.notes: Start exact (end of ST-1 per FDR). End approx from the NIMA 2020 plan (wall shared with D). Width ~3.2-4.0 m (tapered). The FDR component table calls the upstream end '19-ID-B'; the 2020 plan labels this room 19-ID-C. The FDR optics text itself puts BDA-V in 'enclosure C' and BDA-H in 'enclosure D' (r1).

enclosures.name: 19-ID-D
enclosures.role: aperture hutch 2: horizontal BDA at 64 m, photon shutter at 65 m
enclosures.notes: Approx from the NIMA 2020 plan (scaled). The long transport starts at 65.5 m (FDR), so the downstream wall is at ~66 m.

enclosures.name: Long transport corridor
enclosures.role: shielded 4-inch vacuum transport across the experiment hall, through the lab/office (LOM) area and an enclosed corridor to the Long Beamline Building
enclosures.notes: FDR 4-1.2: two long corridors connect the LBB to the APS building and the transports pass through some LOM labs and offices. FDR Fig. 4.1 notes lab reconfiguration for sectors 21 and 22. Ion-pump mini-enclosures at 95, 124, 153 and 183 m.

enclosures.name: 19-ID-E
enclosures.role: experimental station: concrete, temperature-stabilized, vibration-isolated endstation in the Long Beamline Building
enclosures.notes: Internal 14.6 m x 6.6 m with roof ~2.8 m above the beam (NIMA 2020). Start/end estimated from window (213.0) and beamstop (227.0). Walls are 12 in (0.3 m) concrete per MEDSI'20/'25 (the 2020 shielding model assumed 20 cm). Instrument slab is 1 m (3'-3") thick with 0.5 in isolation joints. Adjacent rooms: ISN control area, air lock/vestibule, sample-prep area, wet lab, data closet (MEDSI'25 Fig. 2a). The FDR calls the satellite building 'building 444' (r1, 4-7.7.3).

instruments.name: ISN nanoprobe instrument (19ID-BI-1)
instruments.plain: A scanning X-ray microscope on a granite table. Ultra-stable mirrors in their own clean vacuum box focus the beam to ~20 nm, 6 cm in front of a separate sample chamber. That chamber can be pumped, filled with gas or opened to air while the mirrors stay untouched.
instruments.expert: Optics and sample sit on a common Invar baseplate in separate chambers: UHV for the KB, HV/air/inert gas for the sample. Both have single-crystal diamond windows with a 2 mm He gap between them. Six custom piezo-driven flexure stages on an Invar structure hold the KB pair (KBV 404 mm, KBH 129 mm). It is aligned with a CMM arm, autocollimator and X-ray methods. A 15-channel interferometer measures optics against sample through Zerodur/Invar frames; the metrology loop runs 466 mm down to the Invar base in the 2020 design. The motorized air-bearing granite table, from the APS granite-stage family (r31), becomes monolithic when depressurized. Fly-scanning covers 10x10 mm and 2 kg at 1 mm/s. The rotation stage has capacitive runout correction. Measured KBV pitch noise is 0.4 nrad rms and 1.7 nrad p-p with fiber interferometers in air, pumps off.
detectors: Dectris Eiger2 X 1M on Stäubli TX2-160L robot (XRD/WAXS)
Dectris Eiger2 X 1M on 6 m-travel table (ptychography/SAXS)
sampleEnvironments: High vacuum, air or inert-gas backfill
Hummingbird electrochemical liquid-flow holder (>100 °C, bulk electrodes)
APS closed-cycle He cryostat holder, 40-355 K (in development)

geometryNotes: Source and front end. Two in-line, not canted, revolver undulators share the 19-ID straight, so the beamline sits on the straight-section axis. The HHL front end is windowless. Vertical dogleg in 19-ID-A. M1 (28.0 m) reflects down by 5 mrad and M2 (29.0 m) reflects up by 5 mrad. The beam comes out horizontal again but about 5 mm lower (5 mrad x 1.0 m, my estimate). PM-1 at 29.7 m stops the undeflected white beam. Horizontal optics. The DCM (31.7 m) and DMM (32.7 m) are horizontally deflecting, inboard, small-offset and fixed-exit. They displace the beam sideways but do not change its direction; the offset value is not published. M3 (35.0 m) then deflects 5 mrad inboard. Everything downstream runs on a line rotated 5 mrad inboard of the source axis, which puts the endstation ~0.9 m inboard of the straight-through line at 220 m (185 m x 5 mrad, my estimate, before the mono offset). Hutches. 19-ID-A is the FOE (~23.9-35.8 m), a narrow trapezoid widening downstream. A 12.4 m shielded pipe crosses open floor to 19-ID-C (48.2-~59 m, BDA-V at 55 m). 19-ID-D shares a wall with C (~59-66 m, BDA-H at 64 m, shutter at 65 m). These three are on the experiment-hall floor in the usual APS position outboard of the ring tunnel. Long transport. From 65.5 to 213 m the 4-inch pipe continues in a straight line. It leaves the experiment floor, crosses the lab/office module (LOM) area that serves sectors 21-22, and runs in an enclosed corridor to the Long Beamline Building (LBB) outside the ring building. Shielded ion-pump stations sit at 95, 124, 153 and 183 m, i.e. every ~29 m (FDR); the 2018 vacuum model also had smaller pumps at each end of the 146 m pipe (r26). The exact point where it leaves the building is not published; FDR Figs. 4.1 and 4.48 are schematic. Long Beamline Building. The LBB (building 444 in the FDR; ~24,000 sq ft, r37) is shared with HEXM (20-ID); the same project built the Activated Materials Laboratory next to HEXM (r23). The two long beamlines come from adjacent sectors, so their transports diverge by ~9° (360°/40 sectors); ISN is the lower one in the FDR plan, HEXM the upper. Endstation 19-ID-E. A concrete hutch, 14.6 x 6.6 m inside, with 12 in walls and roof ~2.8 m above the beam. It sits on a separate 1 m isolated slab, with the control area, airlock, sample-prep area and wet lab alongside. Inside, along the beam: window, filters, beam-conditioning granite blocks, fast shutter, then the UHV KB chamber on a granite table. The focus is 61 mm past the KBH end. Then come the separate sample chamber with a robot-mounted XRD detector above and outboard (Be dome tipped 10° up and 25° outboard), the green 6 m ptychography detector table, and the beamstop on the downstream wall. KB direction. KBV reflects upward in the MEDSI'25 drawing, raising the focus ~2 mm above the incoming beam; the FDR schematic draws a downward-facing mirror. KBH deflects horizontally by 5 mrad, direction not published. Scale cue for 3D: everything from 24 m to 66 m is about 42 m of floor; the next 147 m is just pipe.

interactiveIdeas.title: The pinhole trade-off: buying coherence with photons
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors drive two slits (BDA-V at 55 m, BDA-H at 64 m) with sliders and an energy dial (5-30 keV). A live panel shows the beam on each slit (a secondary-source blob ≈6.5 µm tall and ≈28 µm wide FWHM for the as-built M3 position; the 2017 PDR, with the horizontal mirror at 43 m, had ~4-7 µm by ~16-18 µm), the fraction of light that passes, the coherence of the light reaching the 1 mm-wide KB mirror, and the resulting focal spot and flux. Closing the slits sharpens the spot until it hits the diffraction limit, then only costs photons.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why nanoprobes deliberately throw away most of the beam, why the 'secondary source' makes the focus immune to wobbling upstream optics, and why the brighter, smaller APS-U source means much less is thrown away.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Coherence-matched aperture: Δ ≈ 0.44 λ z / A, with A = L·sinθ (KB acceptance). V: z ≈ 165 m, A ≈ 404 mm x 2.5 mrad ≈ 1.01 mm → Δ_V ≈ 3.6 µm at 25 keV, 8.9 µm at 10 keV. H: z ≈ 155.9 m, A ≈ 0.32 mm → Δ_H ≈ 10.5 µm at 25 keV, 26 µm at 10 keV. FDR minimum aperture is ~3.5-4 µm. Demagnification: 1/417 (V), 1/1242 (H), so a 4 µm slit images to ~10 nm (V) and a 13 µm slit to ~10 nm (H). Spot ≈ quadrature sum of the slit image and the diffraction limit (plus figure-error blur). Opening past the secondary-source size adds no flux. Geometric estimate for the flat-beam source (σx 14.5 µm, σy 3.1 µm): V ≈ 7.2 µm x 26/29 ≈ 6.5 µm FWHM; H ≈ 34 µm x 29/35 ≈ 28 µm FWHM with M3 at 35 m (PDR: 4.4-6.6 µm V, 16-18 µm H with the mirror at 43 m). Round-beam mode makes the V blob ~2.7x larger. FDR anchors: coherent 16x16 nm at 3.4e11 ph/s vs open 24x30 nm at 3.1e12 ph/s (25 keV).

interactiveIdeas.title: Why 220 meters? Spot size vs working distance
interactiveIdeas.concept: A side view of the KB mirror pair with draggable mirror length and working distance (5-100 mm), and an energy dial. The display shows the focal spot, the cone angle (NA) and a cartoon in situ cell that either fits in the gap or collides with the mirror. A second panel moves the BDA-to-mirror distance: shorten the beamline and the slit must close to sub-micrometer sizes to keep a long mirror coherently lit, so flux collapses.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: For a given spot size, more working distance needs a longer mirror. A longer mirror needs a wider coherent beam, which needs a longer beamline. That chain is why ISN has its own building.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Diffraction-limited FWHM ≈ 0.88 λ q / (L sinθ) with q = L/2 + W (X. Shi 2016, r27). With L_H = 129 mm, q = 125.5 mm, θ = 2.5 mrad: 17 nm at 25 keV, 42 nm at 10 keV, ~88 nm at 4.8 keV. Spot ∝ λ, so low energies give bigger spots. NA ≈ half the angular spread of rays leaving the mirror ≈ 1.7 mrad. Coherent illumination requires Δ ≤ 0.44 λ z / (L sinθ); for Δ ≈ 3.6 µm at 25 keV, a 1 mm acceptance needs z ≈ 165 m (≈185 m for Δ = 4 µm). Pitfalls: grazing-incidence reflectivity cut-off of Pt at ~2.5 mrad near 30-40 keV; the FDR fixes θ at 2.5 mrad. The 2.5 mrad angle is set by Pt: its critical angle is ≈ 84 mrad·keV / E (my estimate from δ), i.e. ≈2.5 mrad near 34 keV, just above the 30 keV top of the range.

interactiveIdeas.title: The nanoradian challenge
interactiveIdeas.concept: A giant lever arm game: visitors tilt a virtual KB mirror with a knob whose smallest step is 1 nrad and watch the 20 nm spot drift across a sample of nanoparticles. Toggle 'heater on' (a 0.01 °C change on a 50 mm steel support) and footsteps in the hall to see what moves the spot, then switch on the real ISN fixes: Invar/Zerodur frames, an isolated 1 m slab, air socks and interferometers.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How tiny angular errors become nanometer blur, and why the endstation is a building-scale vibration and thermal engineering project.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Spot shift ≈ 2·Δθ·q. KBV: 2 x 5 nrad x 0.396 m ≈ 4 nm (20% of 20 nm); KBH: 2 x 16 nrad x 0.1255 m ≈ 4 nm. These match the stated 5/16 nrad requirements. Measured KBV noise is 0.4 nrad rms, 1.7 nrad p-p. 5 nrad = 5 mm tilt over 1,000 km. Thermal expansion: steel α ≈ 12e-6/K, so 50 mm x 0.01 K ≈ 6 nm; Invar α ≈ 1e-6/K → ≈0.5 nm. Requirements: air ±0.05 °C/h, surfaces ±0.01 °C/h, VC-G 0.78 µm/s rms (1-100 Hz).

interactiveIdeas.title: One pixel, five answers
interactiveIdeas.concept: A fly-scan animation over a solar-cell cross-section. Click any pixel to open five synchronized readouts: an XRF spectrum (Cu, In, Ga, Se peaks), a diffraction pattern from the robot detector, a ptychography speckle pattern, an XBIC current trace and an XEOL spectrum. Toggling to a 'map' view assembles each channel into an image, and the visitor finds the defect that kills current.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Multimodal correlative imaging: composition, structure, electrical performance and optical emission measured at the same 20 nm spot at the same instant.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Excitation must exceed the absorption edge: Se K-edge 12.66 keV (Kα 11.22), Ga 10.37 (Kα 9.25), Cu 8.98 (Kα 8.05), In K-edge 27.94 keV (Kα 24.2) or L lines ~3.3-3.9 keV. Choose ~13-15 keV for CIGS K-lines without In-K. At 30 keV K-edges are reachable up to Sn (29.2 keV); heavier elements use L lines. Fly-scan timing: 1 mm/s with 20 nm pixels = 50,000 pixels/s (20 µs dwell), but ptychography needs ≥~60% probe overlap, so with a ~20-30 nm probe the step is ≤ ~8-12 nm and a ~3 kHz frame rate limits the scan to ~25-35 µm/s. It also needs a coherent probe (BDAs closed).

interactiveIdeas.title: Through the window: choosing the energy for an in situ cell
interactiveIdeas.concept: Build a cell: pick window material and thickness (Si3N4, diamond, Kapton), electrolyte depth (0-2 mm water) and gas path, then slide the X-ray energy. Bars show the incident beam surviving to the sample and the fluorescence of a chosen element escaping back to the detector. Low energy makes the sample glow brightly but the light can't get out; high energy goes through everything but some elements can no longer be seen in their K lines.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why ISN uses hard X-rays up to 30 keV plus a large working distance: real environments (liquids, gases, windows) absorb soft X-rays, and both the incoming beam and the outgoing fluorescence must survive.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Beer-Lambert T = exp(-(μ/ρ)ρt). Water μ/ρ ≈ 41.9 cm^2/g (5 keV), 5.33 (10 keV), 0.81 (20 keV), 0.38 (30 keV) (NIST XCOM). So 1 mm water transmits ~1.5% at 5 keV, ~59% at 10 keV, ~92% at 20 keV and ~96% at 30 keV; 200 µm transmits ~43% at 5 keV. Fluorescence escape uses the emission-line energy, not the beam energy (e.g., Fe Kα 6.4 keV through 1 mm water: μ/ρ ≈ 20 cm^2/g, so ≈13%). ISN chambers use single-crystal diamond windows with a 2 mm He gap, and the XRD Be dome is 0.5 mm.

interactiveIdeas.title: Zoom from millimeters to nanometers (hierarchical imaging)
interactiveIdeas.concept: Start with a 10 mm battery electrode or catalyst pellet mapped coarsely, then zoom 3-4 decades to a single 20 nm-resolved particle. A clock shows how long each zoom level takes at ISN fly-scan speeds versus a pre-upgrade nanoprobe. The 'needle in a haystack' is a rare contaminant particle.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why fast scanning plus a large field (10x10 mm, 2 kg cells) matters: the defects that control performance are rare and must be found before they can be studied.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Scan time ≈ (rows) x (row length / speed) + overheads. A 10x10 mm map at 1 µm pixels and 1 mm/s = 10,000 rows x 10 s ≈ 28 h. A 10x10 µm map at 20 nm pixels = 500 rows x 10 ms ≈ 5 s of motion, but counting statistics (flux ~10^11-10^12 ph/s) and detector rates set the real dwell. Stage limits: 1 mm/s horizontal; vertical 1 mm/s only for ROI <90 µm, otherwise 0.1 mm/s. Data volume: ~10 PB/yr planned.

funFacts: ISN is the longest beamline at the APS. Argonne describes it as sitting 720 feet from the storage ring (r24). The instrument is 220 m from the undulator source and the beamstop is at 227 m (r1).
The Long Beamline Building's beamlines are about three times longer than other APS beamlines, roughly two football fields (r23).

ISN predates the MBA upgrade: a 2013 concept already described it (r32). In the 2015 Early Science report the MBA-era optical design was a 180 m beamline (r28). It grew to 220 m so long focusing mirrors could be lit with coherent light while keeping a 5-6 cm working distance (r1, r13), and the 2017 PDR says the final length was chosen so ISN and HEXM could share one satellite building (r3).

During commissioning the vertical focusing mirror held its angle to 0.4 nanoradians rms, measured in air with the vacuum pumps off. That is like tilting a 1,000 km plank by 0.4 mm at the far end (r9; analogy is my arithmetic).
The endstation air is held to ±0.05 °C for an hour and the instrument surfaces to ±0.01 °C. Fabric 'air socks' blow gentle laminar air, and the exhaust fan is kept outside the room (r9).
The microscope room stands on its own 1-meter-thick concrete slab, cut free from the rest of the building by isolation joints, to meet the VC-G vibration criterion of 0.78 µm/s (r9).

The two tiny beam-defining slits can be hit by up to ~11.6 W of focused X-rays when the multilayer monochromator is used (0.2 W with the crystal monochromator). A slit facing the beam head-on would heat past 850 K and be destroyed, so the jaws are designed to take the beam at a grazing angle (r1).
The 404 mm vertical focusing mirror is about 20 million times longer than the spot it makes (my arithmetic from r9).
ISN was expected to generate ~10 petabytes of raw data a year, nearly 15x what the APS's 2-ID-D ptychography, 2-ID-E XRF and Bio-Nanoprobe instruments produced together (~730 TB) (r25).

Before ISN, 19-ID was the Structural Biology Center's protein-crystallography undulator beamline: 2,277 publications came from 19-ID (r21). SBC planned to support users until the APS 'dark' period began in April 2023 (r22). It has since concluded operations and handed over to the multi-beamline eBERlight program (r21).

U.S. Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm cut the ribbon on the Long Beamline Building on 25 July 2022 (r23). Argonne held a ceremonial groundbreaking on 23 July 2020, with construction scheduled to start that fall (r38); Argonne's 2022 release says ground was broken in June 2020 (r23).

The first ISN concept (2013-14, before the MBA upgrade) planned KB mirrors for a 50 nm high-flux spot and zone plates or multilayer Laue lenses for 20 nm (r32). The upgraded source and a 220 m beamline let the final design reach ~20 nm with mirrors alone, keeping a long working distance (r1).
Samples can be cycled from 40 K (−233 °C) to more than 1000 °C, in vacuum, air or flowing gas, while being scanned at up to 1 mm/s (r9).

openQuestions: Final focal spot. Design is 20x20 nm FWHM at 25 keV (FDR, directory). The MRS Fall 2025 and XRM 2026 abstracts state 25-30 nm at 25 keV, and MEDSI'25 says preliminary measurements 'show promise' of 20 nm. No published measured spot or flux at the sample yet.

DMM status. The FDR specifies a Mo/B4C double-multilayer monochromator (19ID-MN-2), and the 2020 FOE drawing shows it. The 2026 Beamline Directory lists only an 'LN2-cooled H-DCM'. It is unclear whether the DMM was installed or commissioned.

Working distance has four published values: 61 mm (optical, MEDSI'20/'25); 60 mm nominal and 55 mm with the KB enclosure (FDR, feature page, 2025-26 abstracts); 47 mm usable in vacuum (MEDSI'20); and '20-50 mm depending on configuration' (Directory). The museum text should say ~55-61 mm optical and less in practice with chambers and detectors.
M3 position. The FDR component table and the 2020 FOE drawing place M3 at 35.0 m inside 19-ID-A. FDR Fig. 4.40 and the 2017 PDR show the horizontal focusing mirror at 43 m. Assume 35 m as built.
FE exit mask: 2x2 mm^2 (FDR ch. 3 and 4) vs 2 (H) x 1 (V) mm (Sunil 2020 shielding study). As-built value unconfirmed.

Enclosure naming and boundaries. The FDR component table refers to transport 'from 19-ID-A to 19-ID-B', but the 2020 shielding plan shows only A, C, D and E; the PDR planned to reuse SBC-era A/B as the FOE. Hutch extents here are scaled from a 2020 drawing (±0.5 m), not an as-built survey.

Instrument distance: 220 m in the FDR, PDR, SPIE 2021, MEDSI'25 and Directory, versus 210 m in MEDSI'20 and 250 m (820 ft) in Argonne's July 2020 groundbreaking release (r38) and a contractor page. 220 m is adopted. The as-built KB numbers (p = 165.004 m, q = 396 mm) put the focus at 220.4 m if BDA-V is at exactly 55.0 m, or BDA-V at 54.6 m if the focus is at 220.0 m.

Undulator description. FDR ch. 4 says 'a revolver undulator of 4.6 m length'; FDR ch. 3 and the 2026 ID table show two in-line ~2.35 m revolvers (U21/U25 each). Whether an active phase shifter is installed between them at 19-ID is not confirmed publicly.

SPIE 2021 abstract quotes coherent flux 'above 4x10^12 ph/s at 5 keV, and 6x10^12 ph/s at 30 keV'. That is inconsistent with FDR Table 4.51 (4.7x10^11 ph/s at 25 keV after the BDAs) and may be a transcription error. FDR values are used here.
KB reflection directions. MEDSI'25 Fig. 5a shows KBV reflecting upward; FDR Fig. 4.50 draws it facing down. KBH inboard/outboard direction is not published. DCM/DMM lateral offset is not published.

Operating mode. Flat-beam vs round-beam storage-ring mode changes the vertical source size (3.1 vs 8.3 µm rms) and so the BDA-V settings and coherent flux. Which mode is standard for 2026 user runs was not confirmed here.
Endstation wall thickness: 12 in concrete (MEDSI'20, MEDSI'25 Fig. 2b) vs 20 cm assumed in the 2020 shielding model. 12 in is taken as as-built.

Status nuance. The Directory says 'Operational/Accepting General Users' (Oct 2026), but a July 2026 job posting still cites commissioning. The scope of the general-user program (techniques and environments offered) is not documented publicly.

Horizontal secondary-source size. With M3 at 35 m (as built) the 64 m BDA-H sees the source at ~0.83x, about 28 µm FWHM in flat-beam mode (my estimate), not the ~16-18 µm quoted in the 2017 PDR for a mirror at 43 m. The FDR's '~11 km' M3 radius also matches the 43 m layout. Measured BDA-plane beam sizes are not published.

Construction start of the LBB: ceremonial groundbreaking 23 Jul 2020 with construction 'scheduled to begin this fall' (r38) versus 'broke ground for construction in June 2020' in the 2022 release (r23).
As-built KB figure-error spec '<2.0 nm' (MEDSI'25 Fig. 5a) does not state rms or peak-to-valley; the FDR rms targets were 0.38/0.45 nm. Coating (FDR: Pt) is not restated in the as-built paper.

verification.summary: Checked 66 claims against primary sources fetched directly (FDR ch. 3/4, PDR ch. 3/6, MEDSI'18/'20/'25 papers, MEDSI'18 talk, NIMA 2020 accepted manuscript, APS directory, ID table, SR parameters, APS-U updates and progress graphics, MRS/XRM abstracts, computing strategy, HPCwire, Phys.org, HDR, SBC, Europe PMC/OpenAlex/OSTI abstracts). Four MEDSI'25 figures were added.
